title: The dancing peacock
hookLine: a peacock dances without modesty and loses his bride (Jataka 32)

cards: Every bird in the mountains has gathered in one place. The king of the birds, a golden goose, has promised his daughter she may choose her own husband, and she walks along the rows of feathered hopefuls.
She stops in front of the peacock, with his jewel-colored neck and patterned tail, and says: that one. In the Nacca Jataka, that should be the end. It's the beginning of his mistake.

teach.h: A LION, A FISH, A GOLDEN GOOSE.
teach.b: First, the setting. Long ago, the tale says, the four-footed animals made the lion their king, the fish chose a great fish, and the birds chose the golden goose. His daughter asks one wish: to pick her husband herself.
He agrees, and calls the assembly. Second, the choice.
She picks the peacock. The other birds bring him the news, and he's so thrilled, so eager to show what he's got, that he says: she hasn't even seen my dancing yet. Third, the dance.

teach.h: HE DANCES IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.
teach.b: Right there, in front of the king, the bride, and every bird in the mountains, the peacock spreads his feathers wide and dances.
He's so busy showing off that he forgets himself and loses every bit of modesty, in the middle of the crowd. Fourth, the cost. The golden goose is embarrassed for everyone.
He speaks a verse: your voice is pleasant, your back is lovely, your neck has the color of a jewel, but for that dance I won't give you my daughter.

teach.h: GIVEN TO THE YOUNG GOOSE INSTEAD.
teach.b: He has no shame inside and no restraint outside, the king says, and gives his daughter to a young goose, his own nephew. The peacock flies off, ashamed.
The tale never says he was ugly, or unworthy, or unloved. He'd already been chosen. The win was finished, and the urge to prove it is what undid it.
The Jataka tells it for a monk who forgot restraint in front of everyone.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the Nacca Jataka as a lesson in restraint and a sense of shame, hiri and ottappa in Pali.

o: not needing to show off what you have

she chose him; the king even praises his voice, back and neck in his verse.

games.q: you're the peacock. the golden goose's daughter has just chosen you in front of every bird in the mountains. what now?
o: thank her quietly and go to the king.
dance, so everyone sees what she's getting.
ask to see the other suitors' feathers.
games.why: he dances right there, loses all modesty, and the king gives his daughter to a young goose instead.

practice: Recall a place where you're tempted to show off: a meeting, a dinner table, a post you're about to share.
Notice the little lift in the chest, the urge to make sure everyone sees, and without scolding it, feel it rise and pass the way a breath does. Whatever is already settled can stay settled.

wordCard.voice: Modesty. What the peacock lost, dancing to show off after he was already chosen, and so lost the bride he'd already won. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the dance cost him. What's already won doesn't need a dance. Day eight hundred twenty-two, done.
